skills.name: android-testing-setup
skills.description: Analyze and create a testing strategy for native Android apps - install testing libraries, set up test infrastructure, create harnesses for unit tests, UI tests, screenshot tests, and end-to-end tests.

skills.name: architect
skills.description: Sketch types, signatures, and module structure before code, design it at least twice, then stay in the loop while implementation fills in the sketch. Use for "architect this", "design this", a change that crosses a module or service boundary, or non-trivial work where jumping to code would lock in the wrong shape.

skills.name: arena
skills.description: Run N parallel candidates at the same task against a declared rubric, cross-judge them, pick a base, and graft the strongest parts of the losers into it. Use for "arena this", design bakeoffs, or when one attempt at a non-trivial artifact would lock in the wrong shape. The result is one synthesized artifact. Not for coverage or mechanical races that return a report; use `swarm`.

skills.name: benchmark-checklist
skills.description: Vet a perf measurement (limiter, tuning, limits, errors, repeatability, relevance, and whether the work happened) before you report or act on it. Use when you run a benchmark or report a speedup or regression you measured.

skills.name: blast-radius
skills.description: Find what a change could break somewhere else before it ships, beyond the diff, and prove the one fact it is safe because of by running real code instead of writing it up. Use for 'blast radius of X', 'what could this break', or reviewing a small diff you do not trust. Not for a general quality review of the change (use `change-review`), a whole-repository audit (use `repo-audit`), or a threat model and secrets review (use `security-audit`).

skills.name: change-review
skills.description: Use whenever the user asks to review a change before it lands: a PR, a branch, a commit, or uncommitted work. Checks whether the logic is right, safe, holds under real load, is tested where risky, is fast enough, and needs every line, reading the connected code and not only the diff. Use for 'review this', 'review my PR', 'look over this before I merge', or 'is this over-engineered'. Not for a whole repository (use `repo-audit`), a threat model or secrets sweep (use `security-audit`), or running code to prove what a small change breaks elsewhere (use `blast-radius`); for adversarial, run-proven findings use `interrogate`.

skills.name: conventional-commit
skills.description: Use whenever you write a commit message, including when the user asks you to commit or describe staged changes. Writes it in the Conventional Commits format (type(scope): subject, body, breaking-change footer) and picks the type from what the diff does. Not for branch, push, or PR policy; follow the repository's AGENTS.md for those.

skills.name: correct
skills.description: Find the mistakes agents keep repeating in this repo and make each one impossible. Try architecture first, then types, then a lint whose error names the fix, then a test, and write docs last. Prove each check fails on a real past mistake. Repeat this each time the operator corrects you. Use for /correct.

skills.name: create-formal-verification-skill
skills.description: Generate a project-local skill that formally verifies the code where a bug costs the most and tests reach the least, in any language, with whichever verification tool fits. Use for /create-formal-verification-skill, "model-check this race", "prove this invariant", or when concurrency, retries, state machines, parsers, or unsafe code need more than tests.

skills.name: create-pr
skills.description: Create Pull Requests following best conventions. Use when opening PRs, writing or editing PR descriptions, or preparing changes for review. Not for committing (use `conventional-commit`), reviewing a diff (use `change-review`), or merging (use `default-mode` and its shipping playbook).

skills.name: create-verification-skill
skills.description: Generate a project-local verification skill that drives your app the way a user does — any language, framework, or platform. Use for /create-verification-skill, "make a control skill for this repo", or when a project has no scripted way to prove UI/CLI/service behavior. For a one-off browser check of a web app use webapp-testing.

skills.name: default-mode
skills.description: Use first for multi-step engineering that no narrower skill owns: a feature built end to end, a migration, or a plan carried through with checks. Picks a task playbook, sets a verifiable outcome, and checks the result. Also the way in to the workflows the user starts by name: competing attempts judged against a rubric (`arena`), parallel workers over many slices (`swarm`), adversarial stress tests (`interrogate`), and an auditable playbook for a large migration (`figure-it-out`). Do not load on top of a more specific skill.

skills.name: figure-it-out
skills.description: Design an auditable playbook when no narrower one fits - a large migration, an ambitious multi-part change, or work a human reviews after stepping away. Scales rigor to the task, runs a hypothesis loop, and logs decisions. Use for "figure it out" or work too large for a single default-mode playbook. Not for work one existing playbook covers; use `default-mode`.

skills.name: frontend-design
skills.description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.

skills.name: how
skills.description: Explain how a codebase or subsystem works at the level of a senior engineer onboarding onto it - architecture, runtime flow, where things live, and gotchas. Use for "how does X work", code walkthroughs before changing something, and placement or ownership questions ("where should this live", "which package owns this", "is this the right layer"). Not for motivation or history; use `why`.

skills.name: if-u-are-fable-5-2
skills.description: Load once at the start of non-trivial work when your harness names you as Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2). Corrects this model's documented habits. Not for any other model.

skills.name: if-u-are-gpt-5-6-luna
skills.description: Load once at the start of a task when your harness names you as GPT-5.6 Luna (gpt-5.6-luna), including as a subagent. Applies OpenAI's GPT-5.6 guidance to the small tier. Not for any other model.

skills.name: if-u-are-gpt-6-1-sol
skills.description: Load once at the start of non-trivial work when your harness names you as GPT-6.1 Sol (gpt-6.1-sol). Applies OpenAI's GPT-6 family guidance to this model. Not for any other model.

skills.name: if-u-are-gpt-6-astra
skills.description: Load once at the start of non-trivial work when your harness names you as GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra). Corrects this model's documented habits. Not for any other model.

skills.name: if-u-are-haiku-5-5
skills.description: Load once at the start of a task when your harness names you as Claude Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5), including as a subagent. Corrects this model's documented habits. Not for any other model.

skills.name: if-u-are-opus-5-5
skills.description: Load once at the start of non-trivial work when your harness names you as Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5). Corrects this model's documented habits. Not for any other model.

skills.name: in-your-own-words
skills.description: Restate in your own words what you think the user's goals are and what problem they're trying to solve. Use for /in-your-own-words.

skills.name: interrogate
skills.description: Adversarial review where independent adversaries try to break a change or design, and only findings proven by a run survive. Use for "interrogate", "adversarial review", "multi-model review", "challenge this", "stress test this", "find blind spots", or "tear this apart". Not for routine diff review (use `change-review`) or security-focused audits (use `security-audit`).

skills.name: ketchup
skills.description: Catch the user up on what changed in this chat since their last message, in plain words and small visuals. List every item waiting on them with what they need to decide it from the reply alone. Use for /ketchup.

skills.name: ketchup-video
skills.description: Catch the user up like /ketchup, with a short subtitled video of slides for what happened and the waiting calls as text under it. Use for /ketchup-video.

skills.name: maintain-formal-verification-skill
skills.description: Bring a project's formal verification back in line with the code after the code changes: find the commits that touched verified code, update the model, harness, or properties to describe the code as it is now, rerun, and say whether each failure is drift in the verification or a bug in the code. Use for /maintain-formal-verification-skill, "is the model still true to the code", or after merges and refactors that touched verified code without rechecking it.

skills.name: maintain-verification-skill
skills.description: Periodic pass that keeps a project's verification skill and feature map honest: parallel source readers per feature, one live session driving every feature, at most one PR of proven corrections. Use for /maintain-verification-skill or "audit the verify skill".

skills.name: md-docs
skills.description: Use whenever the user wants a repository's context or contributor files created or brought up to date: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, or DOCS.md, including after a layout change or when a repo has none. Not for general markdown editing or sentence-level prose style; use `technical-writing`.

skills.name: pin-rule
skills.description: Pin a rule the user states in chat so it survives context compaction and long sessions. Use when the user says to always or never do something for this project or for all work, or asks to remember a rule. Not for facts or preferences the user did not state as a rule; those belong in memory.

skills.name: principle-attack-the-premise
skills.description: Apply when two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.

skills.name: principle-boundary-discipline
skills.description: Apply when building or changing anything that accepts outside input (HTTP service, CLI, config, external API), including validation, error handling, identifiers, and framework adapters. Concentrate guards at system boundaries (CLI, config, network, external APIs); trust internal types and keep business logic in pure functions.

skills.name: principle-build-the-lever
skills.description: Use when a change repeats one mechanical edit across many sites, when a manual check must be done more than once, or when a reviewer needs to rerun the proof. Build the codemod, script, generator, or check that does or proves it instead of working by hand. Not for a single-line edit.

skills.name: principle-encode-lessons-in-structure
skills.description: Apply when you catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time, or notice a recurring correction. Encode the rule as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

skills.name: principle-exhaust-design-space
skills.description: Apply when a novel interaction or architecture decision has no useful precedent. Build two or three competing prototypes and compare them before committing.

skills.name: principle-experience-first
skills.description: Apply when product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs come up. Choose user delight over implementation convenience; ship fewer polished features over more rough ones.

skills.name: principle-explain-the-number
skills.description: Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

skills.name: principle-fix-root-causes
skills.description: Apply when debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.

skills.name: principle-foundational-thinking
skills.description: Apply before writing logic: choosing core types and data structures, sequencing scaffold-vs-feature work, asking what concurrent actors share. Get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious.

skills.name: principle-guard-the-context-window
skills.description: Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.

skills.name: principle-laziness-protocol
skills.description: Apply when refactoring, sizing a diff, or feeling tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Prefer deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.

skills.name: principle-make-operations-idempotent
skills.description: Apply when designing commands, lifecycle steps, or processing loops that run amid crashes, restarts, and retries. Converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs.

skills.name: principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
skills.description: Apply when introducing a new internal API while old callers still exist. Migrate callers and delete the old API in the same wave instead of preserving compatibility layers.

skills.name: principle-minimize-reader-load
skills.description: Apply when reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers between question and answer, and hidden state in the reader's head; collapse one-caller wrappers and shrink mutable scope.

skills.name: principle-model-the-domain
skills.description: Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files.

skills.name: principle-never-block-on-human
skills.description: Apply when tempted to ask whether to take a reversible action that the task already authorizes.

skills.name: principle-outcome-oriented-execution
skills.description: Apply during planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture; don't preserve smooth intermediate states with throwaway compatibility code.

skills.name: principle-prove-it-works
skills.description: Use before saying any feature, fix, migration, or interface change is done, and whenever the user asks for proof it works. Run the feature the way a user would, read the actual value or output, and show it; a self-report or 'it compiles' is not proof. Probe input-accepting surfaces with hostile inputs (empty, oversized, non-ASCII, concurrent, unsupported).

skills.name: principle-redesign-from-first-principles
skills.description: Apply when integrating a new requirement into an existing design.

skills.name: principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state
skills.description: Apply when concurrent actors might write to the same file, branch, key, or state object. Eliminate the sharing first; serialize structurally only when one shared writer is a real invariant.

skills.name: principle-sequence-verifiable-units
skills.description: Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer.

skills.name: principle-subtract-before-add
skills.description: Apply when sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead code, redundant validators, and stub references before building on the base.

skills.name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
skills.description: Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.

skills.name: principle-type-system-discipline
skills.description: Apply when designing types, reviewing a function signature, or writing code in any statically-typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand semantic primitives, parse external data at boundaries, exhaust variants, derive from authoritative schemas.

skills.name: recall
skills.description: Reconstruct recent work on a named project or topic from earlier agent sessions and shared repository records, including prior decisions, PRs, reversions, and next steps. Use for "catch me up on X", "what have I been working on", or "where did I leave off" across sessions. For only the current chat use ketchup; for resuming one exact branch or session use the session-pickup playbook.

skills.name: reflect
skills.description: Mine a completed or failed agent episode for durable learnings with three parallel reviewers (judgment, tooling, divergent) and a synthesizer, then route each accepted learning to a concrete edit on an existing skill, with rejected and backlog items listed separately. Use when the user says reflect, or after a long task whose recipe should be captured. Not for measuring or promoting learnings across many episodes; use `continual-learning`.

skills.name: reframe
skills.description: Teach the expert words for what the user is building, borrow words from neighboring fields that solved the same problem, then rewrite their description with them. Use for /reframe, when the user cannot name what they want. Not for deepening an already clear prompt; that is sharpen.

skills.name: repo-audit
skills.description: Quality audit of a whole repo or folder: bugs, security holes, what breaks under real load, risky code without tests, slow paths, and what to delete, merge or split. Ranked, each finding explained in plain English. One-shot report, changes nothing. Use for "audit this codebase", "review the whole repo", "find bloat", or "what can I delete". Not for one diff, commit or PR (use `change-review`), a dedicated threat model or secrets review (use `security-audit`), or proving by running code what a small change breaks elsewhere (use `blast-radius`).

skills.name: security-audit
skills.description: Security review of a repository or change - threat model, secrets, dependencies, authentication and authorization, injection, and unsafe data handling - where every finding comes with proof and a fix. Use for "security audit", "is this safe", threat modeling, pre-release security checks, or reviewing auth, input handling, or secrets. Not for a general quality audit of the whole repository (use `repo-audit`), a correctness and quality review of one diff or PR (use `change-review`), or proving what a small change breaks elsewhere (use `blast-radius`).

skills.name: sharpen
skills.description: Make a task deeper, not bigger, then rewrite the prompt. Use for /sharpen.

skills.name: shortcut-debt
skills.description: List every `shortcut:` comment as a debt ledger. One-shot report, changes nothing. Use for "shortcut debt" or "list the shortcuts".

skills.name: show-me-your-work
skills.description: Keep a reviewable decision trail for long-running or unattended work - a TSV log with one row per decision (what, why, evidence, result) - then audit it against the transcript and have an independent reviewer flag what needs attention. Local by default; commit it when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. Use for autonomous or multi-phase runs, or work a human reviews after stepping away. Not for short single-step tasks that need no trail.

skills.name: statechart
skills.description: Check a TLA+ model of a system that moves between states, such as a product flow, a protocol, or a service, and draw it as a Mermaid statechart. The report gives the shortest path to each state that breaks a rule. Use for /statechart, or to show a bug as a path through states.

skills.name: swarm
skills.description: Fan out N parallel workers across independent coverage slices or identical race attempts, drain them, and return one evidence-backed report. Use for "swarm this", parallel coverage, audits, races, gauntlets, or exploration. Not for competing designs that need a rubric, a judge, and grafting into one artifact; use `arena`.

skills.name: tdd
skills.description: Use whenever you fix a bug that a test can reproduce cheaply, and whenever the user asks for TDD, a failing test, or a regression test first. Write a focused test, watch it fail for the right reason, then fix the code. Not for unclear, expensive, integration-heavy, or unrequested test paths; run the closest executable check instead.

skills.name: teach
skills.description: Explain a body of work plainly so a person actually understands it. Runs the `how` and `why` skills and weaves what they find into one clear explanation. Use for 'teach me this', 'help me really understand X', 'explain this change or subsystem to me'.

skills.name: technical-writing
skills.description: Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages. Not for choosing or maintaining project context files; use md-docs.

skills.name: typescript-best-practices
skills.description: TypeScript best practices. Use when reading or editing any .ts or .tsx file.

skills.name: unslop
skills.description: Use whenever prose reads AI-generated or the user asks to humanize, de-slop, or make text sound like a person wrote it: removes filler, inflated vocabulary, em dashes, vague attributions, mannered metaphor, and over-compression while keeping meaning and tone. Also use before delivering docs, commit messages, PR bodies, or announcements. Not for restructuring documents; use `technical-writing` or `md-docs`.

skills.name: webapp-testing
skills.description: Host-neutral browser QA that proves a web app works the way a user would: start the app, drive flows in a real browser with Playwright using role and label locators, assert what the user sees and what the system stored, and keep screenshots, console errors, and failed requests as rerunnable evidence. Use for QA of a web UI, reproducing a browser bug, writing or fixing Playwright tests, or verifying a frontend change. Not for a reusable project harness; use create-verification-skill.

skills.name: why
skills.description: Use whenever the user asks why code, a design, or a number is the way it is: design rationale, tradeoffs, a regression, or a threshold someone chose. Answers from the record, not from reading the code: git history and PRs, issues, docs, and other evidence, cited and with facts kept apart from inference. Not for what code does at runtime (use `how`) or for what a change would break (use `blast-radius`).

skills.name: agent-completion
skills.description: Use whenever an agent says it finished, deployed, fixed, or ran something and you need to know what really happened. Sorts the work into attempted, executed, verified, partial, blocked, and failed from the tool calls and side effects, before a handoff or a done report. Use it even if the user only asks whether the agent's claim is true. For test-driven changes use `tdd` (cstack plugin); for diff review use `change-review` (cstack plugin).

skills.name: agent-context
skills.description: Keep long-running agent work coherent with bounded phases, capped outputs, checkpoints, compact handoffs, and loop detection. Use for large repositories, many tool calls, compaction, repeated reads, or delegated work. Not for short tasks that fit in one pass.

skills.name: agent-evaluation
skills.description: Use whenever someone wants to know if a model, prompt, skill, hook, or agent configuration is actually better: designs and runs repeated representative tasks and compares outcome, trajectory, reliability, cost, latency, and cleanup. Use it even when the user just asks 'is the new config better?'. Not for a single code test. To compare independent alternatives use `arena` (cstack plugin); to promote learnings across episodes use `continual-learning`.

skills.name: agent-harness
skills.description: Use whenever the work is the runtime around a model-driven agent rather than application code: the agent loop, model adapter, tool registry, context handling, permissions, orchestration, or verification. Covers building a custom loop around a local model, debugging tool calls that loop or vanish between turns, and changes to Codex, Claude Code, Pi, or other coding-agent harnesses. Not for ordinary application code.

skills.name: continual-learning
skills.description: Help an agent improve its reusable skills, rules, and memory from ordered task experience with audit, replay, transfer checks, and retirement. Use when a learning should persist across many episodes and its retention must be measured. Not for mining one episode into skill edits; use `reflect` (cstack plugin).

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Finds and installs agent skills from the open skills ecosystem with the `npx skills` CLI. Use only when the user asks to find or install a skill, such as "find a skill for X" or "is there a skill that can...". Not for ordinary how-to questions or for skills already in this pack; read those directly.

skills.name: multi-agent-workflow
skills.description: Use whenever work is split across two or more agents or subagents: parallel research, review, or implementation with isolated ownership, explicit handoffs, and independent verification of what each returns. Use it even if the user only says 'have a few agents look at this'. Not for short, sequential, or shared-state tasks (stay direct), same-task alternatives (use `arena` (cstack plugin)), or coverage slices over a large surface (use `swarm` (cstack plugin)).

skills.name: prompt-audit
skills.description: Audit skills, rules, AGENTS files, hooks, tool descriptions, and agent configuration for stale model-specific cruft, conflicts, broken paths, and over-steering. Use before editing or after a model or host release. Not for code review (use `change-review` (cstack plugin)) or for writing a new skill from scratch (use `default-mode` (cstack plugin) and its authoring-a-skill playbook).

skills.name: tool-orchestration
skills.description: Use whenever many tool or API calls make a task slow or fragile: decides which calls run directly, in parallel, programmatically, asynchronously, or as an offline batch, from their dependencies, side effects, and latency. Not for building the runtime loop (`agent-harness`) or for fanning out whole agents (`multi-agent-workflow`).

skills.name: bitsandbytes-quantization
skills.description: Use whenever a model does not fit in GPU memory or needs cheaper inference: quantize LLMs to 8-bit or 4-bit (INT8, NF4, FP4) with bitsandbytes and Hugging Face Transformers, check the accuracy cost, or set up QLoRA training and 8-bit optimizers. Use it even if the user only says the model is too big for their GPU. Not for CPU-only inference (GGUF) or production serving throughput (GPTQ/AWQ).

skills.name: literature-review
skills.description: Find, read, and synthesize primary research papers for a technical or scientific question, verify every citation, and record each claim with its evaluation conditions. Use for literature reviews, related work, "what does the research say", choosing a method from papers, or checking a cited claim.

skills.name: peft-lora-qlora
skills.description: Use whenever someone fine-tunes a large language model on limited GPU memory: LoRA, QLoRA, and other PEFT methods for 7B to 70B models, including target modules, rank and alpha, training config, adapter merging, and multi-adapter serving with Hugging Face PEFT. Use it even if the user only names a model and a GPU size.

skills.name: scientific-slides
skills.description: Use when building or reviewing research/scientific slide decks (conference talks, seminars, defenses) — minimal text, one idea per slide, visual hierarchy, data/results slides, timing, and visual review. Works with PowerPoint, Google Slides, and Beamer.

skills.name: scientific-visualization
skills.description: Use whenever you make or fix figures for a paper, thesis, or report in Matplotlib, Seaborn, or Plotly: multi-panel layouts, error bars and uncertainty, missing data, colorblind-safe color and contrast, misleading axes, and journal export. Use it even if the user only says the plots look amateur.

skills.name: write-kaggle-benchmarks
skills.description: Write, push, run, publish, and manage Kaggle Benchmark tasks using the kaggle CLI and the kaggle-benchmarks Python SDK. Use when the user wants to create or push a benchmark task (optionally with attached Kaggle datasets), run benchmarks against LLM models, check task/run status, stream or fetch execution logs, download results and source notebooks, publish a task to make it public, or troubleshoot benchmark workflows.
